issues.legal_issue: The government may exercise suo motu revisional power over an order granting permission to use land for non-agricultural purposes.
material_facts: The Collector granted permission to use the land for the proposed project for non-agricultural purposes.
The government initiated revision on its own motion and cancelled the permission.
The cancellation was challenged in court.
issues.conclusion: The government had power to revise the Collector’s order suo motu, and the Court found no reason to interfere with the High Court’s conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: The Court upheld the High Court’s interpretation of sections 44 and 257 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966: the government’s revisional power under section 257 extended to orders passed by the Collector, including an order granting permission under section 44. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.collector_granted_land_use_permission: A Collector granted permission to use land for a specified purpose.
predicates.government_started_revision_on_its_own_m: The government initiated review of the Collector’s order without an application by a party.
predicates.challenge_to_suo_motu_revision: A party challenged in court the government’s revision of the Collector’s order on its own motion.

issues.definition: When a party challenges the government’s own-motion review of a Collector’s land-use permission, the rule permits the government to revise that order.

issues.legal_issue: Cancellation of a land-use permission through revision may be upheld when the government acted bona fide on grounds that existed in the public interest, even if it did not act diligently.
material_facts: The proposed plant was to be located beside a river used by nearby inhabitants for drinking and washing.
Villagers objected that effluent from the plant would pollute the river and endanger public health and the livelihood of local residents.
The government investigated the objections, issued a show-cause notice, and cancelled the permission through revision.
Violent riots later occurred in opposition to the proposed plant.
The High Court found that the grounds relied on by the government existed and that its action was bona fide and in the public interest, although the government had not acted diligently.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the cancellation of the permission, accepting the High Court’s conclusion that the government acted bona fide and in the public interest on grounds that existed.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 44 and 257 of the Maharashtra Land Revenue Code, 1966, the government could revise the Collector’s permission; the Court upheld the cancellation where the grounds for the government’s bona fide public-interest action existed. The government’s lack of diligence did not require the cancellation to be set aside, though it supported compensation. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.challenge_to_revisional_cancellation: A party asked a court to set aside a government decision cancelling a land-use permission through revision.
predicates.government_acted_on_public_interest_conc: The government based its cancellation decision on concerns raised about effects on the public.
predicates.water_pollution_risk: The proposed activity was alleged to risk polluting water used by people for drinking or other essential purposes.
predicates.serious_public_order_concerns: The proposed activity was associated with serious opposition or public disorder.

issues.definition: When a revisional cancellation is challenged and the government acted on public-interest concerns that include a water-pollution risk or serious public-order concerns, the rule permits the cancellation to be upheld as bona fide public-interest action.

issues.legal_issue: A person whose project permission is cancelled in the public interest may receive compensation for costs incurred on the project and interest on that compensation where the government did not act diligently.
material_facts: The project proponents incurred costs in setting up the project after receiving permission to use the land.
The government later cancelled the permission in the public interest.
The High Court found that the government had not acted diligently and directed compensation for project costs incurred up to the show-cause notice.
The Supreme Court maintained the compensation direction and modified it to include interest on the compensation amount for the period after the notice.
issues.conclusion: The project proponents were entitled to compensation for costs incurred on the project up to the show-cause notice and to interest on the compensation amount for the subsequent period.
issues.legal_principle: The Court maintained compensation for project costs while upholding the government’s public-interest cancellation, and modified the High Court’s order to provide interest on the compensation amount for the period after the show-cause notice. The basis stated was the government’s lack of diligence; no statutory compensation provision or earlier case was relied on.

predicates.permission_cancelled_in_public_interest: The government cancelled permission for a project on public-interest grounds.
predicates.project_costs_incurred_before_cancellati: The project proponents incurred costs on the project before receiving notice that the permission was under review for cancellation.
predicates.government_did_not_act_diligently: The government failed to act diligently in handling the matter before cancelling the permission.

issues.definition: When permission is cancelled in the public interest after project costs have been incurred and the government did not act diligently, the rule provides compensation and interest to the project proponents.
